extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science / comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative observations for judging the design and functioning of national (particularly American) constitutional institutions, with comparative references to European systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of choosing the President
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's method of selecting the President (presidential electors chosen by the people rather than a simple popular vote or choice by Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framers intended electors as judicious persons to avoid evils of a popular vote and Congress selecting the chief magistrate. In practice electors have become 'mere cyphers' and the President is practically chosen by the people at large; the electoral machinery now chiefly prevents a simple national majority and makes pivotal States decisive. (See I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of the presidential election format
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical consequences of having a practically simultaneous popular vote for President every four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elections involve tremendous expenditure of energy, time, and money, and induce a crisis which, if coincident with powerful public passions, may be dangerous to the commonwealth. (See II.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of disputed presidential outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The vulnerability of an elective executive system to doubtful, fraudulent, or violent election results and the difficulty of finding a trusted authority to settle disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputed results may leave the question unsettled until the pre-existing executive has ceased to have a right to obedience; the election of 1876 illustrates these dangers. This risk is inherent in systems with popular election of the executive and is greater where the executive is chosen by the people rather than by Chambers. (See III.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnover of executive officers and policy discontinuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent change of higher (and many lower) executive officers—typically once in four years—creates jerks in machinery and discontinuity of policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change produces either loss of responsibility or efficiency during a President's final months; outgoing Presidents may be reckless or weak because of diminished incentives; secretaries may lack influence in foreign relations near term end. (See IV.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and function of the Vice-Presidency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President's office is of little ordinary importance yet is the constitutional successor to the Presidency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the office is unimportant in day-to-day function, candidates are often chosen for party reasons and may be second-rate; upon succession such a person may prove capable (Arthur) or disastrous (Andrew Johnson). The position is therefore 'ill-conceived.' (See V.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuity of Congressional policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress often exhibits discontinuous policy-making and lacks continuity in legislation and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes include frequent turnover of members, committee fragmentation, lack of recognized leaders, and tendency to take up and drop measures across sessions; continuity that exists relies on broad maxims or settled national principles. (Item in VI; expanded guidance follows under 'maintenance of continuous policy'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of legislative control over officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the legislature has sufficient mechanisms to control administrative officials and hold them accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book notes a 'want of adequate control over officials' as a defect, tied to Congress's limited competence and lack of leadership or guiding committees to ensure administrative reforms and amending statutes are introduced or passed. (Item in VI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive opportunity to influence the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the executive has avenues to influence legislation and secure needed laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the American system ministers lack the regular means (as in Europe) to get proposed statutory amendments attended to by the legislature; an American minister depends on committee favour and has no command of a majority. (Item in VI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to secure passage of necessary legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there exists any authority charged with ensuring that legislation the country needs is passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of a body charged to secure passage of necessary measures is listed as a defect; in parliamentary systems ministers can introduce and usually pass non-controversial administrative amendments, an advantage lacking in the U.S. system. (Item in VI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of disputes among co-ordinate powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency for disputes to arise between the President, the Senate, and the House and the resulting friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The divided and balanced powers create opportunities for conflict and deadlock among the three co-ordinate branches; such disputes add to systemic friction. (Item in VI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of continuous policy in popular governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of maintaining a general and continuous policy in popular representative systems, especially the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular American causes: executive and many lower officers change every four years; one House changes every two years; neither House recognizes permanent leaders; there need be no accord between Congress and executive; absence of a 'party in power' in the European sense; little true leadership; cabinets lack authority over Congress; legislative action fragmented across committees. These structural features impede continuous cabinet and legislative policy and the enactment of administrative reforms. (Item in VI and subsequent explanation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnover and lack of permanent leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Short terms and regular turnover in offices and the absence of permanent leaders reduce effective governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists as specific obstacles: exec change every four years, one House change every two years, no recognized permanent leaders, and inability to dissolve Parliament to enforce discipline — all undermine leadership and continuity. (Supporting detail to VI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives ought to be chosen from among the best men of the country and, if possible, its natural leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of four essentials to an excellent representative system; the author notes Americans generally fail on this point—Congressmen are not chosen from the best citizens. (First of the 'four essentials'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative responsibility to constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives should be strictly and palpably responsible to their constituents for their speeches and votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the second of four essentials; surprisingly responsibility is not fully realized in America. Causes include committee system, lack of organized party leadership, and candidate selection methods. (Second of the 'four essentials'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative independence and courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives should have courage to resist momentary impulses of constituents and act as representatives rather than mere delegates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third of the four essentials; Americans are said not to attain this—members mostly deem themselves delegates rather than leaders. (Third of the 'four essentials'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflex action of legislature upon the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature and its members should have a reflex action on the people: while deriving authority from them, they should educate and inform the public by the experience and superior knowledge they acquire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fourth of the four essentials; the author finds Americans also lacking here—the reciprocal action between electors and Congress is not sufficiently close or delicate; citizens often cannot feel they advance particular measures by their vote. (Fourth of the 'four essentials'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence and its vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Life-tenure and insulation of the judiciary are merits, but the federal judiciary remains vulnerable to attacks if the legislature and executive combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature can change number of justices; President may appoint persons with political bias; together they may obtain desired constitutional determinations. The only safeguard mentioned is public disapproval. (See VIII.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for organic/historical development over artificial devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional features that are natural outgrowths of old institutions and habits tend to be more successful than distinctly artificial devices consciously introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues American failures tend to be where devices (election of President/VP by electors ad hoc) are artificial rather than rooted in tradition; recommends gradual small improvements made conformably to existing conditions over large bold experiments. (Discussion following VIII.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principles: sovereignty of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should embody the principle that the supreme law is the direct utterance of the people's will, that they alone can amend it, and that powers not delegated are reserved to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All main features of American government can be deduced from this principle: constitution supremacy, delegated powers only, and legal responsibility of organs to the people. (Stated as one of two main principles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principles: distrust of government agents (checks and balances)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional design based on distrust of various organs and agents of government, safeguarding States and citizens and subjecting agents to oversight by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distrust leads to careful safeguards against aggression by central government and creates jealous observers among organs (executive, legislature, judiciary) to restrain abuses—explains the elaborate system of checks and balances in the U.S. frame. (Stated as the second of two main principles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of public opinion and patriotism as informal safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Good sense and patriotism of the people, embodied in usages and traditions, are essential to make free government work despite institutional defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that informal forces—public opinion, patriotism, traditions—are stronger in America than in Europe and often remedy systemic faults in times of difficulty; constitutions rely on these for practical functioning. (Discussion near end of chapter.)
